status: source-admission pilot; not a prophecy ranking

admissionRule.prohibitedPromotion: A case failing pre_event_source or independent_outcome cannot validate foresight.

cases.label: Nahum and the fall of Nineveh

sourceDate.basis: The fall of Thebes supplies a common lower boundary; the relationship of the book to Nineveh's 612 BCE fall remains compositionally disputed.

cases.rejectionReceipt: The present dating interval touches the event boundary; the pilot has not established a securely pre-event textual form independent of the predicted fall.

cases.label: Jeremiah's seventy years for Babylon

sourceDate.basis: The oracles are placed in the late seventh or early sixth century BCE, while compositional and textual-layer questions remain material.

outcome.label: fall of Babylon and early Persian return policy

cases.rejectionReceipt: Babylonian domination, Jerusalem's destruction, exile and return supply different admissible endpoints; the textual forms and seventy-year semantics require a source-layer audit before scoring.

cases.label: Ezekiel, Nebuchadnezzar and Tyre

sourceDate.basis: The book internally dates the Tyre oracle and a later oracle that says Nebuchadnezzar's army received no wages from Tyre.

outcome.label: end of Nebuchadnezzar's long siege without the plainly expected spoil

cases.rejectionReceipt: This is admitted as an adverse interpretation-and-repair case, not yet as predictive calibration; source layers and the relation between Nebuchadnezzar and later Alexander receptions must remain separate.

cases.label: Daniel 11 and the death of Antiochus IV

sourceDate.basis: The detailed Seleucid sequence and the divergence around Antiochus IV's death make composition date part of the hypothesis rather than settled metadata.

cases.rejectionReceipt: The source-date inference is entangled with the apparent transition from accurate sequence to inaccurate endpoint; it is a control for ex-eventu identification, not an independent prediction witness.

cases.label: Jeremiah's short-horizon oracle against Hananiah

sourceDate.basis: The narrative places prediction and death in the same year; the surviving literary record is later and supplies both sides.

outcome.label: death of Hananiah in the seventh month

cases.rejectionReceipt: Excellent internal test form, but the same narrative reports oracle and outcome; it can train annotation, not establish foresight.

cases.label: Mark 13 and the destruction of the Temple

sourceDate.basis: Common composition ranges straddle the destruction of the Second Temple.

outcome.label: Roman destruction of Jerusalem and the Second Temple

cases.rejectionReceipt: A source-date interval spanning AD 70 cannot independently validate pre-event prediction without an earlier securely dated textual witness or source layer.

cases.label: Agabus and the Claudian famine

sourceDate.basis: Acts' common composition ranges postdate the Claudian famine it narrates.

outcome.label: severe famine affecting Judaea under Claudius

cases.rejectionReceipt: External famine evidence can support historical retrodiction, but the surviving prophecy report postdates the event and cannot validate foresight.

cases.label: Newton's 2060 lower bound

sourceDate.basis: The surviving private calculation postdates Newton's 1705 knighthood and predates his death.

outcome.label: end of the 1260-year period and associated eschatological transition

cases.censoring: right-censored; the asserted lower bound has not yet been reached as of 2026-10-28
cases.rejectionReceipt: Open forecasts cannot calibrate a rule; the unbounded 'may end later' clause also prevents 2060 from acting as a terminal falsification date.
